title: Comfort in discomfort: A systematic review of pain perception in ultrarunners
description: Pain is an inherent and expected consequence of ultrarunning (distances >42.2km). Pain perception encompasses how individuals interpret feelings of pain. Here, we systematically reviewed studies of pain management and coping, pain tolerance and threshold, experience of pain, and the impacts of pain perception on performance, within an ultrarunning context. We searched five electronic databases (MEDLINE, PsychINFO, Scopus, SportDiscus, and Web of Science), complemented with citation searches. A total 433 studies were screened, with 36 included in this review. Findings indicate that perceived pain increases during and after ultrarunning, with changes to pain intensity, sensitivity, and modulation. Pharmacological and physical interventions employed to manage pain show mixed effectiveness, with minimal impact on performance. Alternatively, maladaptive cognitive coping strategies increase the degree to which pain subjectively interferes with ultrarunning, time spent thinking about pain, and likelihood of race withdrawal, but experiential awareness reduces pain interference. Ultrarunners exhibit higher pain tolerance than non-athletes, derive moral value from pain, and actively distinguish between ‘good’ (expected) and ‘bad’ (injury-related) pain. The ability to effectively appraise manage, and tolerate pain is considered a key differentiator of high and low performing ultrarunners. Acknowledging that pain is not a unidimensional physiological phenomenon, directions for future research are discussed.

title: Signaling social identity in referential communication
description: Any choice of words simultaneously conveys information about the world and, at the same time, conveys information about the speaker, revealing aspects of their social identity. In this paper, we investigate how speakers strategically modify referential language to signal group membership. Across four experiments using a minimal referential communication paradigm, we find that speakers with the explicit goal of signaling social affiliation (1) choose more concise utterances, (2) preferentially select group-specific referents and descriptions, and (3) resist the otherwise strong tendency to be understood by everyone in the audience. Standard models of referential communication that focus on the trade-off between informativity and efficiency cannot explain these patterns; we argue instead for a model where speakers trade off the referential utility of being understood against the social utility of being identified as an in-group member.

title: Fear of Negative Evaluation as a Core Predictor of Eating Disorder Risk in Adolescents: A Sex-Based Analysis
description:
Background: Eating disorders (ED) commonly emerge during adolescence, a developmental period characterised by heightened sensitivity to social evaluation. Fear of negative evaluation (FNE), a core feature of social anxiety, may represent a key mechanism underlying vulnerability to disordered eating. This study examined FNE as a predictor of ED psychopathology in a non-clinical sample of adolescents and tested whether this relationship differs by sex.
Methods: 192 adolescents aged 16–19 completed standardised self-report measures of eating disorder symptoms (Eating Disorder Diagnostic Scale-5) and FNE (Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation Scale- revised) as part of a larger online survey. 
Results: FNE emerged as a significant and robust predictor of ED symptoms (b = 0.40, 95% CI [0.30, 0.51], p < .001), accounting for approximately a third of the variance in ED symptom scores (R² = .32–.34). Females reported significantly higher FNE and ED symptoms than males (Mann-Whitney U tests, medium effect sizes), but the relationship between FNE and ED symptoms did not significantly differ by sex (FNE × Sex interaction, b = −.13, p = .228).
Conclusions: Findings support FNE as a key predictor of ED psychopathology in adolescents. Elevated sensitivity to social judgement appears to increase vulnerability to disordered eating similarly across sexes, even though females carry a disproportionately higher burden of both FNE and ED symptoms. Targeting FNE in early intervention and prevention efforts, particularly among adolescent females, may offer a promising avenue for reducing ED risk.

title: Attachment and Caregiving as Social Allostatic Inference: An Updated Social Neuroscience Account from Single Brains to Dyads
description: Humans are highly social, and much of that sociality is regulatory: individuals manage the demands placed upon their bodies not only alone but through and with others. Attachment science has pursued how the brain accomplishes this for the better part of a century, and its most recent contribution has been neurobiological. Within the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt) programme, we previously specified a neuroanatomical architecture of two interacting systems and four domain-general modules for organised attachment, extended it to attachment disruption and disorganisation, and moved it from single brains to dyads through hyperscanning as part of Relational Neuroscience. What that work established energetically, through social allostasis, it did not specify computationally. Here we close that gap. Drawing on active inference, allostasis as interoceptive inference, and recent constructs of attachment as prediction, we propose the term social allostatic inference: the attachment system is one predictive-allostatic loop, the four modules are its successive stages, and organised, disrupted, and disorganised attachment are characteristic settings of the precision parameters that govern it. We extend the account to the caregiving system, which shares this architecture but infers rather than senses both the error that initiates its loop and the signal that terminates it. At the level of the dyad, interpersonal neural and bio-behavioural synchrony are read as indices of where regulatory work is invested rather than of bond quality directly. We address persistent misconceptions in trauma-informed practice and set out a measurement programme.

title: Top-down versus bottom-up theories of phonological acquisition: A big data approach
description: Recent work has made available a number of standardized meta-analyses bearing on various aspects of infant language processing.   We  utilize  data  from  two  such  meta-analyses (discrimination of vowel contrasts and word segmentation,  i.e.,  recognition of word forms extracted from running speech) to assess whether the published body of empirical evidence supports a bottom-up versus a top-down theory of early phonological development by leveling the power of results from thousands of infants.   We predicted that if infants can rely purely on auditory experience to develop their phonological categories, then vowel discrimination and word segmentation should develop in parallel,  with  the  latter  being  potentially  lagged  compared  to the  former.   However,  if  infants  crucially  rely  on  word  form information to build their phonological categories, then development at the word level must precede the acquisition of native sound categories.  Our results do not support the latter prediction.   We discuss potential implications and limitations,  most saliently that word forms are only one topdown level proposed to affect phonological development, with other proposals suggesting that top-down pressures emerge from lexical (i.e., word-meaning pairs) development. This investigation also highlights general procedures by which standardized meta-analyses may be reused to answer theoretical questions spanning across phenomena.

title: Vaccination as Collective Action During a Pandemic: Evidence from 6.1 Million COVID-19 Vaccination Records in Denmark
description: Classical theories in health psychology explain individuals’ decisions about whether or not to engage in protective behavior such as vaccination during a health emergency as guided by trade-offs about personal risks and benefits. Yet, vaccinations involve a clear collective action component, where individuals can protect others by getting vaccinated, beyond the personal benefits. Following recent research, we develop the argument that individual differences in the motivation to engage in collective action should influence vaccination decisions during the most significant health emergency in the 21st century, the COVID-19 pandemic, above and beyond the predictors proposed by classical theories. We test this argument by combining survey observations from 380,516 unique Danish adults with population-wide registry data on COVID-19 vaccination status for 6.1 million individuals in Denmark, of whom 4.9 million received at least one vaccine dose. Using this unique data infrastructure, we compare classical psychological correlates of protective behavior with psychological measures of individual-differences in collective action motivation. The results demonstrate collective action motivation was more strongly associated with vaccination behavior than threat appraisal or coping appraisal across the vaccination sequence, spanning completion of the recommended primary vaccination course, booster receipt, time to full vaccination, and vaccination uptake among the children of survey respondents. Furthermore, high levels of collective action motivation strongly weakened the role of personal considerations that would otherwise deter vaccination uptake, both in terms of whether or not the individual gets vaccinated and how quickly the individual gets vaccinated. These findings provide important information on the prerequisites of successful vaccination campaigns during major health crises and how governments and authorities can facilitate them.

title: Uneven Effects of Decision Stakes on Advice Integration
description:
People often rely on human or AI advice, but whether higher stakes improve advice
integration remains unclear. Across two preregistered experiments (N = 99), participants
combined perceptual judgments with advice from artificial agents while stakes varied up to
twenty-fold. A Bayesian model provided benchmarks for optimal advice weighting. Higher
stakes prolonged deliberation but did not, on average, improve advice weighting or decision
accuracy. Instead, their effects were uneven and varied with cognitive ability. Participants
with higher ability became more optimal and accurate under high stakes, whereas those
with lower ability performed worse. Thus, incentives can mobilize effort without uniformly
improving performance and may widen differences between decision-makers. These findings
show that insufficient motivation alone cannot explain suboptimal advice integration
and identify cognitive capacity as a boundary condition on the benefits of higher stakes in
assisted decision-making.

title: 90% mental, 10% physical? Psychological and physiological predictors of ultrarunning performance
description: Within the ultrarunning community, performance is often considered ‘90% mental, 10% physical’. This demonstrates the influence of both psychological and physiological factors, particularly emphasising the perceived dominance of psychology. However, extant research typically considers psychological or physiological variables in isolation. Additionally, studies frequently recruit participants from a single ultramarathon, thereby neglecting heterogeneity between events. The current study addresses these limitations by employing an interdisciplinary approach and recruiting participants from a range of races to develop a robust, predictive model of ultrarunning performance. Ultramarathon participants (n = 69 across 24 events) underwent graded exercise testing, psychometric surveys, and physiological/cognitive assessments (Cold Pressor, Stop-Signal, and Serial Sevens tasks). Performance was quantified as percentile finishing time relative to gender-matched event winners. Selection of the initial 15 candidate variables was informed by evidence from relevant literature. A single global model was developed using backwards stepwise regression (Aikake Information Criterion selection), including four covariates: age, gender, apparatus, and distance. The overall model (p < .001, adj. r2 = .426) included VO2max (ß = .609), emotional intelligence (ß = .281), inhibitory control (ß = .259), and sleep behaviours (ß = .226) as key significant predictors. These results demonstrate that the predictability of ultrarunning performance is improved by moving beyond traditional metrics of fitness and considering both psychological and physiological variables. Overall, this model provides an integrated approach for maximising endurance sports training and performance, with broader application to other fields involving physical and psychological exertion (e.g., military, pain management).

title: Facial expression synchrony is associated with neural synchrony during mother-infant interactions
description: Social interactions depend on the temporal coordination of multiple behavioral and neural processes. This coordination, known as interpersonal synchrony, is thought to support communication and shared understanding, yet how different synchrony modalities relate to one another remains unclear. Here we examined facial expression and neural synchrony during naturalistic play in 86 mother–infant dyads (infant age 7.4 months). Facial expression synchrony was quantified using automated facial action unit coding and windowed cross-lagged correlations, while neural synchrony was assessed using functional near-infrared spectroscopy and wavelet-transform coherence across prefrontal and temporo-parietal regions. Mothers and infants showed strong facial expression synchrony, during approximately 40 % of the interaction and consistent neural synchrony across cortical regions. The two synchrony modalities were related, but associations were localized and bidirectional, suggesting that synchrony across modalities does not arise from a single underlying process. Instead, synchrony may emerge from multiple interacting systems that support flexible social exchange.

title: Self-Assessed, but Not Experimentally Induced, Rejection Sensitivity Predicts Eating Disorder Symptoms in Adolescent Girls
description:
Objective: Social rejection is a salient stressor during adolescence, a peak period for eating disorder (ED) onset. This study examined whether self-reported rejection sensitivity and affective responses to experimentally induced ostracism were associated with one another, and whether each independently predicted ED psychopathology, in non-clinical adolescent girls.
Method: Forty-seven girls aged 13–14 completed Cyberball and the Needs-Threat Scale (NTS), the Online and Offline Social Sensitivity Scale (O²S³), the Eating Disorder Diagnostic Scale-5 (EDDS), and the Autism Spectrum Quotient-10 (AQ-10). Partial correlation and multiple linear regression, controlling for autistic traits, examined associations between NTS, O²S³ and EDDS scores.
Results: NTS and O²S³ scores were positively correlated after controlling for AQ-10 (r = .37, p = .009). NTS, O²S³ and AQ-10 together predicted EDDS scores (R² = .32, p < .001); O²S³ was an independent predictor (β = .43, p = .003), whereas NTS was not (β = .24, p = .104).
Discussion: Self-assessed rejection sensitivity, rather than affective responses to induced ostracism, was associated with ED psychopathology, suggesting that subjective appraisal of everyday social rejection may be more clinically relevant than acute, laboratory-induced exclusion. Rejection sensitivity may represent a useful target for early ED intervention in adolescent girls.

title: Parsing Exposure to Adversity: How does Caregiving Deprivation Pose a Unique Risk to Children's Adjustment?
description: Children’s emotion perspective taking and social problem-solving are regarded as key social-cognitive mechanisms through which adverse parenting increases children’s vulnerability to social and behavioral problems. Guided by the Dimensional Model of Adversity and Psychopathology (DMAP), this study examined whether parenting threat and deprivation operate selectively or commonly through children’s emotion perspective taking and social problem-solving to increase risk to their social (i.e., peer relationship quality) and behavioral (i.e., externalizing symptomology) wellbeing. Participants included 238 children, primary caregivers, and their partners with the first of three annual measurement occasions occurring during the transition to formal school (Mean age = 4, 52% female; 68% White; 18% Black; 16% Latine, 10% multiracial, and 4% another race). Parenting deprivation and threat were assessed observationally across multiple parent-child interaction tasks. Children’s social-cognitive mechanisms were assessed using validated tasks, and teachers completed surveys of child psychological problems. Results from the fully lagged cascade model indicated that parental deprivation selectively predicted children’s subsequent social problem-solving and emotion perspective taking difficulties over and above the influence of parental threat. In the latter part of the cascade, children’s diminished emotion perspective taking predicted increases in externalizing symptoms, while children’s blunted social problem-solving predicted diminished social competence.

title: Mental Health Supports for Caregivers of Autistic Children: An Umbrella Review
description:
Objective: Caregivers of Autistic children commonly report reduced mental health and wellbeing in comparison to caregivers of non-autistic children. Extensive research has demonstrated that psychological interventions improve caregiver mental health. This umbrella review aimed to (1) assess the quality and validity of systematic reviews and/or meta-analyses (SRs) that evaluated the effectiveness of clinician-delivered, non-pharmacological interventions on mental health and wellbeing outcomes in caregivers of Autistic children, and (2) synthesise evidence on the overall effectiveness of these interventions.
Method: The review was conducted in line with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for umbrella reviews. Risk of bias was assessed using the Risk of Bias in Systematic Reviews tool. 
Results: The search across seven databases identified 2227 potentially eligible records. Seventeen SRs were included, comprising n = 61 relevant primary studies and n = 1515 participating caregivers. Methodological quality of the included SRs was generally low. No SRs were considered authoritative sources for practice recommendations. Assessment of relevant studies from included SRs identified Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and psychoeducation as demonstrating the most consistent positive impact on caregivers’ self-reported symptoms of anxiety, depression, and stress, as well as quality of life, and general mental health and wellbeing. Mindfulness and cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) interventions also appeared to improve symptoms in most domains to an extent, though more inconsistently.
Conclusion: Despite the poor quality of available SRs, assessment of individual studies identified ACT and psychoeducation as broad intervention modalities that strengthen caregiver psychological wellbeing. Research, practice, and policy implications are discussed.
